incoming.name: Mongolia
incoming.excerpt: Mongolia has rich mineral resources, and copper, coal, molybdenum, tin, tungsten, and gold account for a large part of industrial production.

incoming.name: Rocky Mountains
incoming.excerpt: Minerals found in the Rocky Mountains include significant deposits of copper, gold, lead, molybdenum, silver, tungsten, and zinc.

outgoing.name: 19th century
outgoing.excerpt: Molybdenum was little used and remained in the laboratory until the late 19th century.

outgoing.name: Aircraft
outgoing.excerpt: Molybdenum is used in oil pipelines, aircraft and missile parts, and in filaments.

outgoing.name: Corrosion
outgoing.excerpt: Special molybdenum-containing alloys, such as the Hastelloys, are notably heat-resistant and corrosion-resistant.

outgoing.name: Mineral
outgoing.excerpt: Though molybdenum is found in such minerals as wulfenite (PbMoO4) or powellite (CaMoO4), the main commercial source of molybdenum is molybdenite (MoS2).

outgoing.name: Soil
outgoing.excerpt: There is a trace requirement for molybdenum in plants, and soils can be barren due to molybdenum deficiencies.

outgoing.name: Sweden
outgoing.excerpt: In 1996, an increase in acid rain near Uppsala, Sweden caused a depletion in the natural foods of moose in nearby rural areas.

outgoing.name: United States
outgoing.excerpt: About half of the world's molybdenum is mined in the United States, with Phelps Dodge Corporation being a primary provider.

outgoing.name: United States dollar
outgoing.excerpt: The market for Mo-99 products is estimated to be on the order of US$100 million per year.

outgoing.name: World War I
outgoing.excerpt: Molybdenum use soared during World War I, when demand for tungsten (Wolfram) made tungsten scarce and high-strength steels were at a premium.
